---
title: "Q-Value"
description: "An estimate of the expected cumulative reward for taking an action in a state and then following a policy."
term: "Q-Value"
letter: "Q"
category: "Reinforcement Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

A Q-value estimates how good it is for an agent to take a particular action
in a particular situation, considering both the immediate reward and what
may happen afterward.

## Technical explanation

The action-value function $Q^\pi(s,a)$ is the expected discounted return
when action $a$ is taken in state $s$ and subsequent actions follow policy
$\pi$. The optimal action-value function $Q^*(s,a)$ assumes optimal
decisions thereafter. Q-values may be represented in a table or approximated
by a neural network.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Q-values help an agent compare actions and are central to methods such as
Q-learning and deep Q-networks. Their reliability depends on sufficient,
representative experience and appropriate learning and exploration choices.

## How it works

An agent estimates values from observed rewards and successor states. A
temporal-difference target often combines the immediate reward with a
discounted estimate of future value. Choosing the highest Q-value is greedy
with respect to the current estimates, but exploration may deliberately
choose other actions.

## Practical example

In a grid-world, the Q-value for moving right from one cell estimates the
total discounted reward expected after that move. The agent can compare it
with values for moving left, up, or down when selecting an action.

## Common misconceptions

- A Q-value is not necessarily a probability and can be negative or greater
  than one.
- The estimated value can be wrong or uncertain; selecting the largest
  estimate does not guarantee the best real outcome.
